unresolved: The requested investment-product responsibility provision, associated footnote, incorporated requirements and applicable version remain unverified. Their wording is needed to distinguish retained responsibility, prescribed conduct, required outcomes and any combination, and to establish incident, materiality, timing, escalation, remediation and cure thresholds. The intermediary circular expressly refers readers to the separate investment-product circular; this establishes a source dependency, not the missing rule’s content.

The adverse citations address substitution of sources and overstatement of their force, not evidence of an actual breach. The similarly labelled intermediary passage concerns heightened risks of bearer-form securities on public-permissionless networks, not the requested Product Provider standard. Its technical-factor provision suggests consideration of a non-exhaustive list; that wording cannot indiscriminately be converted into mandatory outcome guarantees.

The provider’s identity, regulated capacities, product classification, authorisation, activities and assessment date are unknown. Tokenised Securities are described as traditional securities with a tokenisation wrapper and are a subset of Digital Securities. The treatment of that subset cannot automatically be extended to novel digital arrangements lacking comparable underlying rights or controls.

Allocation and exercise of authority are unproved. Relevant factual inquiries include contracts, delegated functions, vendor mandates, access to records, decision rights, escalation arrangements, powers to require correction and practical ability to intervene. These are proposed inquiries, not a checklist established by the unavailable investment-product rule.

Supervisory conduct is unproved. Evidence would need to identify responsible personnel, expertise and resources, independence where applicable, information examined, product and technology due diligence, risk assessment, review scope and frequency, challenge, findings, escalation, corrective instructions and verified follow-up. An event log alone supplies none of these substantive conclusions.

Ownership and settlement evidence is absent. Relevant matters include governing law, enforceability of token rights and extrinsic rights, any security interest or encumbrance, the authoritative ownership record, effectiveness of transfers, legal settlement finality and the relationship between ledger entries and legal entitlements. The appendix expressly raises these legal questions; technical completion alone does not answer them.

Reconciliation evidence is absent. Needed facts include the records compared, holdings and underlying rights covered, cut-off times, completeness, accuracy, methodology, breaks, outstanding exceptions, investigations and verified corrections. Matching records may share an error. Reconciliation must therefore be distinguished from proof of legally valid ownership and settlement.

Technology and custody facts are unknown. The supplied appendix addresses vendor track records, smart-contract audits and reasonable reliance on third-party audits, network robustness, interoperability, private-key and administrative controls, continuity planning, privacy and money-laundering risks. Its note also recognises that secondary-record blockchain use may require technology audits. Network form, bearer or registered status, key control, custody-chain segregation, omnibus holdings, custodian resources and sub-custodian arrangements determine which considerations matter.

The technical and custodial appendices are delivered and cannot be treated as missing merely because a partial reading said so. Nevertheless, their retained extraction disagreement and unsupported visual content remain provenance limitations. Their technology-audit note does not verify the separately identified missing footnote in the intermediary circular; other referenced network, bearer-form, continuity and complexity qualifications remain unverified.

The Handbook’s delivered general requirements address product names and protection descriptions, distributors, counterparties, service providers and offering-document languages, including a Commission waiver of the bilingual requirement. These distinct duties do not establish the requested tokenisation fulfilment test. The delivered valuation extract, rather than an asserted management-company acceptability extract, supplies valuation-specific obligations; its applicability and current status remain unestablished.

Disclosure and operational adequacy are separate. The intermediary circular expects clear material information about settlement finality, transfer limitations, smart-contract audit status, administrative and continuity controls and custody. Disclosure that an arrangement exists does not prove that it works adequately or fulfils the requested responsibility rule.

The complexity discussion conditions see-through assessment on effective mitigation of technology risks and preserves underlying-security assessment and complex-product suitability requirements. It does not establish a universal incident-free obligation or automatic cure through reconciliation. Existing securities offering and conduct regimes remain relevant, but their complete operative provisions and application to this arrangement are not supplied.

The delivered intermediary text starts a historical discussion of the professional-investor restriction but ends before establishing its subsequent disposition. The partial reading’s claims about removal of that restriction and a virtual-asset threshold clarification are unsupported by the delivered operative text. Their truth is not determined here, and neither claim may support fulfilment of the responsibility requirement.

No incident history, losses, recovery evidence or remediation results are supplied. An incident could implicate conduct, an independently required outcome or reporting requirements, but the applicable rule and facts must establish that consequence. Neither an adverse event nor later correction alone decides compliance or breach.

The retained sources are reconstructed derivatives, not verified complete current law or original HTTP bytes. Exact character preservation does not establish extraction fidelity, rendering, completeness, legal classification or applicability. Metadata, navigation, hashes and inherited parser flags cannot establish duties. Descriptions of historical extracts, judgments, later-treatment searches, an OOXML derivative and broader chapter supplements do not supply additional operative text in this request or establish judicial treatment.

The offered gaps preserve distinct source identities and unresolved locations; none supports a positive proposition. Not every listed location is established as necessary to this question. Further relevance must follow from the governing rule and actual facts, and a similarly labelled location in another source cannot fill a gap. No solver result or mere source presence establishes compliance.

alternatives.condition: The Product Provider is an intermediary issuing, or substantially involved in issuing, Tokenised Securities that it intends to deal in or advise on, and the supplied issuance guidance applies.
alternatives.consequence: It remains responsible for the overall tokenisation arrangement notwithstanding outsourcing. Delegating operations does not itself discharge responsibility. This does not require every operational decision to remain with the provider, nor establish the separate target provision’s meaning. Governing instruments and actual operation must distinguish delegated tasks, decision-making authority and retained legal responsibility.

alternatives.condition: The applicable target standard and scheme terms are established, and contemporaneous evidence demonstrates the required allocation of authority, substantive supervision and operational performance.
alternatives.consequence: That combined evidence could justify fulfilment within its demonstrated scope and period. Reserved powers or nominal responsibility alone would not establish satisfactory performance. Successful outcomes may support, but do not automatically prove, adequate supervision; adverse outcomes require investigation and do not automatically establish breach unless the governing rule makes them decisive.

alternatives.condition: A supervision record demonstrates competent and sufficiently resourced review, appropriate scope and timing, substantive testing against the applicable requirements, and appropriate responses to material findings.
alternatives.consequence: It may support fulfilment of the particular supervisory requirement demonstrated. An entry recording only that supervision occurred establishes neither its adequacy nor compliance throughout the assessment period. Findings, escalation, corrective action and follow-up must be examined where relevant to the governing standard.

alternatives.condition: A reconciliation reliably compares the relevant token records with authoritative records of legally recognised ownership or extrinsic rights, with appropriate completeness, timing and treatment of discrepancies.
alternatives.consequence: It may support record accuracy within the demonstrated scope. The appendix expressly identifies regular reconciliation as one consideration alongside legal validity of underlying ownership and encumbrances. Completion alone proves neither accuracy nor enforceability, settlement finality, effective transfer, absence of unauthorised transfers, adequate supervision or satisfaction of every applicable requirement.

alternatives.condition: The Handbook’s Product Provider requirements apply to the relevant appointments.
alternatives.consequence: The provider must exercise reasonable care and diligence in selecting counterparties and service providers and, after due enquiries, satisfy itself that key appointees have competence and resources to discharge their engagements and comply with specifically applicable product-code requirements. Distributor selection has its own qualification and competence requirement. These duties are not interchangeable with a universal continuing-supervision or discharge test.

alternatives.condition: The actor deals in, advises on, or manages portfolios investing in Tokenised Securities within the supplied intermediaries guidance.
alternatives.consequence: The guidance calls for diligence on issuers, relevant vendors and tokenisation risks, and understanding and satisfaction with ownership and technology controls before engagement. Necessary manpower and expertise and diligence on both the underlying product and technology also matter. These role-specific expectations cannot automatically be attributed to a differently situated Product Provider.

alternatives.condition: The tokenisation-risk guidance and appendix apply to the arrangement.
alternatives.consequence: Relevant non-exhaustive considerations include vendor experience; appropriate technology audits and justified reliance on third-party smart-contract audits; network robustness, consensus and finality risks; interoperability; private-key, cybersecurity and administrative controls; legal enforceability and regulatory approval; continuity planning; privacy; and financial-crime risks. Appropriate technology audits may remain relevant where blockchain is only a secondary record. A reconciliation or supervision entry cannot substitute for this broader assessment.

alternatives.condition: Bearer-form Tokenised Securities use permissionless tokens on a public-permissionless network.
alternatives.consequence: The supplied text identifies heightened cybersecurity, asset-recovery and financial-crime risks. Additional non-exhaustive custody considerations include central-custody immobilisation, transfer time, security, experience, private-key controls, custody-chain segregation, financial resources, conflicts, operational capabilities and permitted sub-custodian selection, appointment and monitoring. The omnibus-client-account qualification concerns segregation from other customers, not an unrestricted exception to segregation from custodian assets. These considerations do not themselves establish discharge.

alternatives.condition: The Handbook management-company acceptability criteria apply.
alternatives.consequence: Relevant investment experience, expertise, demonstrable track records and sufficient time and attention must be assessed. The qualified group-experience route does not remove the individual investment-experience expectation. The text generally expects designated key personnel for both management company and investment delegate and up-to-date records available to the Commission. The incomplete multimanager qualification cannot be reconstructed. Personnel criteria do not independently establish adequate tokenisation supervision.

alternatives.condition: The Handbook valuation requirements apply, including where a third party performs valuation.
alternatives.consequence: The management company’s requirements include appropriate selection, appointment, ongoing monitoring, supervision and periodic review of the third party. Distinct requirements address net-asset-value pricing and disclosed adjustments; independent valuation policies; prevention and correction of pricing errors; periodic review and at least annual competent, functionally independent review including testing; valuation timing and disclosure; diligent, good-faith fair-value adjustments in consultation with the trustee or custodian; and qualified, approved valuation of unquoted investments. A recorded review or apparently correct price alone does not establish all these requirements.

alternatives.condition: The product is an authorised investment product, or actual scheme conditions, modifications or waivers affect the applicable requirements.
alternatives.consequence: The separately referenced authorised-product requirements and actual scheme terms must be established and applied. Their incorporation is a concrete unresolved dependency, not evidence of a universal exemption or a universal discharge standard.

alternatives.condition: The client-information guidance applies and material information is communicated clearly and comprehensibly.
alternatives.consequence: Disclosure concerning settlement finality, transfer restrictions, audit status, administrative controls, continuity planning and custody may satisfy the relevant communication element. Disclosure does not itself establish effective controls, satisfactory audits, adequate supervision or correct ownership records.

alternatives.condition: Technology risks are effectively mitigated and the supplied complexity and distribution guidance applies.
alternatives.consequence: Complexity is assessed through the underlying traditional security, with the incorporated complexity guidance. Complex-product suitability requirements remain applicable irrespective of solicitation or recommendation. Removal of a mandatory professional-investor-only restriction does not remove public-offering requirements: applicable authorisation or prospectus requirements, or a professional-investor or other available exemption, still require assessment.

assumptions: No actual supervision event, reconciliation result, contractual allocation, scheme condition or assessment-period fact is stipulated. Examples are conditional, not findings about conduct.
The supplied intermediaries circular, appendix and Handbook pages concern distinct actors and activities. Their applicability is not inferred merely from the title Product Provider.
The questions have open-corpus scope. Missing material in this delivered selection is not absent from the corpus or law, and no merely imaginable exception is treated as an established dependency.

Partial readings are proposals, not authority. Reconstructed text, inherited normative flags, titles, index metadata and exact character preservation do not independently establish legal classification, extraction fidelity, completeness, currentness or applicability.
value.conclusion: The target-specific authority and applicability bridge remains unresolved. The delivered text does not verify the requested Product Provider responsibility provision or its associated footnote, establish the governing assessment period, or supply the target discharge standard and consequences. It nevertheless supplies concrete conditional rules: a qualifying issuing intermediary retains responsibility despite outsourcing, and applicable Handbook requirements impose distinct appointment, competence, personnel or valuation obligations. Allocation of authority, substantive supervisory conduct and operational or ownership-record outcomes require separate findings. Neither a recorded supervision event nor a completed reconciliation alone establishes adequate supervision, proper ownership records or fulfilment of the target requirement. A justified conclusion would require the applicable standard and scheme terms, the relevant actor and product relationships, and evidence demonstrating the substance, coverage, results and necessary follow-through of the work. This is an insufficiency of the delivered authority and facts, not a finding of compliance, breach, liability or absence of relevant law.

Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products. A. Terminology 5. There is currently no universal definition or taxonomy for categorising tokenised securities and many different structures may exist in the market. For the purpose of this circular, tokenised securities are traditional financial instruments (eg, bonds or funds) that are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO) which utilise DLT (such as blockchain technology) or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Tokenised Securities). 6. Tokenised Securities are a subset of a broader set of digital securities, the latter of which in this circular are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the SFO that utilise DLT or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Digital Securities). Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may be structured in more bespoke, novel or complicated forms, with some existing exclusively on a DLT-based network with no links to extrinsic rights or underlying assets and having no controls to mitigate the risks that ownership rights may not be accurately recorded2. Some of them may fall under the definition of an interest in a CIS. For example, Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may include tokenisation of fractionalised interests in real world or digital assets such as artwork or land in a manner different from a traditional fund but such that the arrangement would amount to a CIS, or tokenisation of a profit sharing arrangement which is not in the form of traditional securities. B. Nature of Tokenised Securities 7. At the outset, given that the nature of Tokenised Securities are fundamentally traditional securities with a tokenisation wrapper, the existing legal and regulatory requirements governing the traditional securities markets continue to apply to Tokenised Securities. In particular, offerings of Tokenised Securities would be subject to the prospectus regime under the Companies (Winding up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32) (C(WUMP)O) and the offers of investments regime under Part IV of the SFO. Conduct of intermediaries in the distribution of or advising on Tokenised Securities, management of Tokenised Securities in the form of tokenised funds, management of funds investing in Tokenised Securities and secondary market trading of Tokenised Securities on virtual asset trading platforms are also governed by existing conduct requirements for securities-related activities. C. New risks arising from tokenisation 8. The overarching principle of the SFC’s regulatory approach is “same business, same risks, same rules”. In addition to complying with existing legal and regulatory requirements applicable to traditional securities, intermediaries should manage the new risks, which are not typically associated with traditional securities, especially ownership risks (eg, how ownership interest relating to the Tokenised Securities is transferred and recorded) and technology risks (eg, forking, blockchain network outages and cybersecurity risks) in activities involving tokenisation. 9. The SFC notes that there are several common archetypes of DLT networks, including: (a) private-permissioned, which is a closed-loop private network characterised by a centralised authority that controls and restricts access to predetermined users, and is typically governed by rules that apply to all users; (b) public-permissioned, which is a public network with a centralised authority that controls and restricts access through authentication, for example; and (c) public-permissionless which is an open, public network that does not restrict access for privileges and has defining characteristics such as decentralisation, pseudonymity and large-scale user base3. Risks vary depending on the type of DLT network used, and should be addressed through the implementation of adequate controls. 10. In the case of Tokenised Securities in bearer form4 issued using permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks, there may be heightened cybersecurity risks. Due to the lack of restrictions

for public access and the open nature of these networks, investors may suffer substantial losses without recourse and may also have practical difficulties recovering their assets or pursuing claims for losses in the event of theft, hacking or other cyberattacks. Further, as a result of such Tokenised Securities’ relative ease of transfer which would result in a change in ownership and their anonymity, they have potentially higher exposures to money laundering and know-your-client issues compared with Tokenised Securities in registered form. D. Considerations for engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities 11. Intermediaries engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities should have the necessary manpower and expertise to understand the nature of such businesses, especially the new risks relating to ownership and technology, and manage such risks appropriately. 12. Intermediaries should act with due skill, care and diligence, and perform due diligence on the Tokenised Securities based on all the available information to identify the key features and risks of the Tokenised Securities. This would include intermediaries’ existing obligation to conduct due diligence on the product itself (eg, on the underlying bond or fund which is being tokenised) and also on the technology aspects given the use of tokenisation technology. Issuance of Tokenised Securities 13. Where intermediaries issue (eg, fund managers of tokenised funds) or are substantially involved in the issuance of the Tokenised Securities which they intend to deal in or advise on, they remain responsible for the overall operation of the tokenisation arrangement notwithstanding any outsourcing to third-party vendors/service providers. 14. In assessing the risks related to the technical and other aspects of Tokenised Securities, an intermediary is suggested to take into account the list of non-exhaustive factors set out in Part A of the Appendix to this circular. 15. For custodial arrangements, intermediaries should take into account the features and risks of the Tokenised Securities in considering the most appropriate custodial arrangement for the Tokenised Securities to manage ownership and technology risks. Additional considerations for the custodial arrangement for bearer form Tokenised Securities which use permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks are set out in Part B of the Appendix to this circular. 16. For tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products, please also refer to the requirements under the Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products issued by the SFC. Dealing in, advising on, or managing portfolios investing in Tokenised Securities 17. Where intermediaries deal in, advise on, or manage portfolios investing in Tokenised Securities, intermediaries are reminded to conduct due diligence on the issuers and their third-party vendors/service providers involved in the tokenisation arrangement as well as the features and risks arising from the tokenisation arrangement. 18. Intermediaries should understand and be satisfied with the controls implemented by the issuers and their third-party vendors/service providers to manage ownership and technology risks of the Tokenised Securities before they engage in related activities. Please refer to Parts A and B of the Appendix to this circular for a non-exhaustive list of factors for consideration. E. Information for clients 19. Intermediaries should make adequate disclosure of relevant material information specific to Tokenised Securities (including the risks of the Tokenised Securities) and communicate such information in a clear and easily comprehensible manner. 20. Intermediaries are expected to provide clients with material information on the tokenisation arrangement, for example: (a) whether off-chain or on-chain settlement is final; (b) the limitations imposed on transfers of the Tokenised Securities (if any); (c) whether a smart contract audit has been conducted before deployment of the smart contract (if any); (d) key administrative controls and business continuity planning for DLT-related events5; and (e) the custodial arrangement (if applicable). Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products. A. Terminology 5. There is currently no universal definition or taxonomy for categorising tokenised securities and many different structures may exist in the market. For the purpose of this circular, tokenised securities are traditional financial instruments (eg, bonds or funds) that are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO) which utilise DLT (such as blockchain technology) or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Tokenised Securities). 6. Tokenised Securities are a subset of a broader set of digital securities, the latter of which in this circular are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the SFO that utilise DLT or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Digital Securities). Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may be structured in more bespoke, novel or complicated forms, with some existing exclusively on a DLT-based network with no links to extrinsic rights or underlying assets and having no controls to mitigate the risks that ownership rights may not be accurately recorded2. Some of them may fall under the definition of an interest in a CIS. For example, Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may include tokenisation of fractionalised interests in real world or digital assets such as artwork or land in a manner different from a traditional fund but such that the arrangement would amount to a CIS, or tokenisation of a profit sharing arrangement which is not in the form of traditional securities. B. Nature of Tokenised Securities 7. At the outset, given that the nature of Tokenised Securities are fundamentally traditional securities with a tokenisation wrapper, the existing legal and regulatory requirements governing the traditional securities markets continue to apply to Tokenised Securities. In particular, offerings of Tokenised Securities would be subject to the prospectus regime under the Companies (Winding up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32) (C(WUMP)O) and the offers of investments regime under Part IV of the SFO. Conduct of intermediaries in the distribution of or advising on Tokenised Securities, management of Tokenised Securities in the form of tokenised funds, management of funds investing in Tokenised Securities and secondary market trading of Tokenised Securities on virtual asset trading platforms are also governed by existing conduct requirements for securities-related activities. C. New risks arising from tokenisation 8. The overarching principle of the SFC’s regulatory approach is “same business, same risks, same rules”. In addition to complying with existing legal and regulatory requirements applicable to traditional securities, intermediaries should manage the new risks, which are not typically associated with traditional securities, especially ownership risks (eg, how ownership interest relating to the Tokenised Securities is transferred and recorded) and technology risks (eg, forking, blockchain network outages and cybersecurity risks) in activities involving tokenisation. 9. The SFC notes that there are several common archetypes of DLT networks, including: (a) private-permissioned, which is a closed-loop private network characterised by a centralised authority that controls and restricts access to predetermined users, and is typically governed by rules that apply to all users; (b) public-permissioned, which is a public network with a centralised authority that controls and restricts access through authentication, for example; and (c) public-permissionless which is an open, public network that does not restrict access for privileges and has defining characteristics such as decentralisation, pseudonymity and large-scale user base3. Risks vary depending on the type of DLT network used, and should be addressed through the implementation of adequate controls. 10. In the case of Tokenised Securities in bearer form4 issued using permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks, there may be heightened cybersecurity risks. Due to the lack of restrictions

for public access and the open nature of these networks, investors may suffer substantial losses without recourse and may also have practical difficulties recovering their assets or pursuing claims for losses in the event of theft, hacking or other cyberattacks. Further, as a result of such Tokenised Securities’ relative ease of transfer which would result in a change in ownership and their anonymity, they have potentially higher exposures to money laundering and know-your-client issues compared with Tokenised Securities in registered form. D. Considerations for engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities 11. Intermediaries engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities should have the necessary manpower and expertise to understand the nature of such businesses, especially the new risks relating to ownership and technology, and manage such risks appropriately. 12. Intermediaries should act with due skill, care and diligence, and perform due diligence on the Tokenised Securities based on all the available information to identify the key features and risks of the Tokenised Securities. This would include intermediaries’ existing obligation to conduct due diligence on the product itself (eg, on the underlying bond or fund which is being tokenised) and also on the technology aspects given the use of tokenisation technology. Issuance of Tokenised Securities 13. Where intermediaries issue (eg, fund managers of tokenised funds) or are substantially involved in the issuance of the Tokenised Securities which they intend to deal in or advise on, they remain responsible for the overall operation of the tokenisation arrangement notwithstanding any outsourcing to third-party vendors/service providers. 14. In assessing the risks related to the technical and other aspects of Tokenised Securities, an intermediary is suggested to take into account the list of non-exhaustive factors set out in Part A of the Appendix to this circular. 15. For custodial arrangements, intermediaries should take into account the features and risks of the Tokenised Securities in considering the most appropriate custodial arrangement for the Tokenised Securities to manage ownership and technology risks. Valuation and pricing

6.11    Offer and redemption prices should be calculated on the basis of the scheme's net asset
        value divided by the number of units/shares outstanding. Such prices should fairly reflect
        the value of a scheme’s assets and may be adjusted by fees and charges, provided the
        amount or method of calculating such fees and charges is clearly disclosed in the
        offering document.

6.11A The management company should establish appropriate policies and procedures for
      independent valuation of each type of assets held by a scheme in consultation with the
      trustee/custodian. Such policies and procedures should seek to detect, prevent and
      correct pricing errors and be consistently applied. The management company should
      review the valuation policies and procedures on a periodic basis to ensure their
      continued appropriateness and effective implementation. The valuation policies,
      procedures and process should be reviewed (at least annually) by a competent and
      functionally-independent party such as a qualified independent third party or a person
      performing an independent audit function.

        Notes: (1)     Where fair value adjustments are necessary in view that market value of
                       a scheme’s assets is unavailable, or reasonably considered to be not
                       reliable or reflective of an exit price upon current sale, the management
                       company shall conduct such adjustments with due skill, care and
                       diligence, and in good faith. The process and conduct of fair value
                       adjustments should be done by the management company in consultation
                       with the trustee/custodian.

               (2)     The management company must comply with all applicable legal and
                       regulatory requirements in respect of the valuation of a scheme’s assets.

               (3)     For the purpose of satisfying the requirement on independent review of
                       valuation policies, procedures and process, the review should include
                       testing the valuation procedures by which scheme assets are valued. The
                       management company shall exercise due skill, care and diligence in the
                       selection of a competent and functionally-independent party.

6.11B Assets of a scheme should be valued on a regular basis and in any event, on the days
      that the scheme’s units/shares are offered or redeemed in accordance with the
      constitutive documents. Valuation frequency and the basis of valuation of a scheme’s
      assets should be clearly disclosed in the offering document.

6.11C Where a third party is engaged in the valuation of a scheme, the management company
      shall exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in the selection, appointment and
      ongoing monitoring of such third party in ensuring such entity possesses the appropriate
      level of knowledge, experience and resources that commensurate with the appropriate
      valuation policies and procedures for each scheme. The valuation activities of such third
      party should be subject to ongoing supervision and periodic review by the management
      company.

        Valuation of unquoted securities

6.12    The value of investments not listed or quoted on a recognized market should be
        determined on a regular basis by a professional person approved by the
        trustee/custodian as qualified to value such investments. Such professional person may,
        with the approval of the trustee/custodian, be the management company.

6.11    Offer and redemption prices should be calculated on the basis of the scheme's net asset
        value divided by the number of units/shares outstanding. Such prices should fairly reflect
        the value of a scheme’s assets and may be adjusted by fees and charges, provided the
        amount or method of calculating such fees and charges is clearly disclosed in the
        offering document.

6.11A The management company should establish appropriate policies and procedures for
      independent valuation of each type of assets held by a scheme in consultation with the
      trustee/custodian. Such policies and procedures should seek to detect, prevent and
      correct pricing errors and be consistently applied. The management company should
      review the valuation policies and procedures on a periodic basis to ensure their
      continued appropriateness and effective implementation. The valuation policies,
      procedures and process should be reviewed (at least annually) by a competent and
      functionally-independent party such as a qualified independent third party or a person
      performing an independent audit function.

                       a scheme’s assets is unavailable, or reasonably considered to be not
                       reliable or reflective of an exit price upon current sale, the management
                       company shall conduct such adjustments with due skill, care and
                       diligence, and in good faith. The process and conduct of fair value
                       adjustments should be done by the management company in consultation
                       with the trustee/custodian.

               (2)     The management company must comply with all applicable legal and
                       regulatory requirements in respect of the valuation of a scheme’s assets.

               (3)     For the purpose of satisfying the requirement on independent review of
                       valuation policies, procedures and process, the review should include
                       testing the valuation procedures by which scheme assets are valued. The
                       management company shall exercise due skill, care and diligence in the
                       selection of a competent and functionally-independent party.

6.11B Assets of a scheme should be valued on a regular basis and in any event, on the days
      that the scheme’s units/shares are offered or redeemed in accordance with the
      constitutive documents. Valuation frequency and the basis of valuation of a scheme’s
      assets should be clearly disclosed in the offering document.

6.11C Where a third party is engaged in the valuation of a scheme, the management company
      shall exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in the selection, appointment and
      ongoing monitoring of such third party in ensuring such entity possesses the appropriate
      level of knowledge, experience and resources that commensurate with the appropriate
      valuation policies and procedures for each scheme. The valuation activities of such third
      party should be subject to ongoing supervision and periodic review by the management
      company.

6.12    The value of investments not listed or quoted on a recognized market should be
        determined on a regular basis by a professional person approved by the
        trustee/custodian as qualified to value such investments. Such professional person may,
        with the approval of the trustee/custodian, be the management company.

Chapter 4: Product Providers
      General duties and obligations

4.1   The Product Provider shall:

      (a)    comply with the applicable provisions of the Handbook;

      (b)    respond to any enquiries made by the Commission in relation to the relevant
             product and the associated matters promptly and in an open and co-operative
             manner;

      (c)    inform the Commission promptly should there be any material breach of the
             Handbook; and

      (d)    use its best endeavours to take appropriate remedial action to rectify any breach
             of the Handbook promptly.

             Note: The main purpose of such remedial action is to ensure that investors are
                   not being put in a disadvantageous position as a result of the breach and
                   to maintain market integrity.

      Conflicts of interest

4.2   The Product Provider shall avoid situations where conflicts of interest may arise including
      any actual or potential conflicts that may arise between different parties in respect of a
      product. Where such a conflict cannot be avoided, and provided that investors interests
      can be sufficiently protected, the conflict shall be managed and minimized by appropriate
      safeguards, measures and product structure and these measures and safeguards shall
      be properly disclosed to investors.

      Name of product

5.1   A products name shall not be undesirable or misleading.

      Notes:        Issuers should consider the following factors before selecting the name for a
                    product:

                    (i)     whether it is inconsistent with the nature of the product or the

                    (ii)    whether the name of the product would give investors a sense of
                            assurance or security not justified by the underlying features of the
                            product;

                    (iii)   whether it might lead investors into thinking or create the impression
                            that persons other than the Product Provider are responsible for the
                            product; and

                    (iv)    whether it might lead investors into thinking or create the impression
                            that the Product Provider is not responsible for the product.

Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products. A. Terminology 5. There is currently no universal definition or taxonomy for categorising tokenised securities and many different structures may exist in the market. For the purpose of this circular, tokenised securities are traditional financial instruments (eg, bonds or funds) that are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO) which utilise DLT (such as blockchain technology) or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Tokenised Securities). 6. Tokenised Securities are a subset of a broader set of digital securities, the latter of which in this circular are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the SFO that utilise DLT or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Digital Securities). Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may be structured in more bespoke, novel or complicated forms, with some existing exclusively on a DLT-based network with no links to extrinsic rights or underlying assets and having no controls to mitigate the risks that ownership rights may not be accurately recorded2. Some of them may fall under the definition of an interest in a CIS. For example, Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may include tokenisation of fractionalised interests in real world or digital assets such as artwork or land in a manner different from a traditional fund but such that the arrangement would amount to a CIS, or tokenisation of a profit sharing arrangement which is not in the form of traditional securities. B. Nature of Tokenised Securities 7. At the outset, given that the nature of Tokenised Securities are fundamentally traditional securities with a tokenisation wrapper, the existing legal and regulatory requirements governing the traditional securities markets continue to apply to Tokenised Securities. In particular, offerings of Tokenised Securities would be subject to the prospectus regime under the Companies (Winding up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32) (C(WUMP)O) and the offers of investments regime under Part IV of the SFO. Conduct of intermediaries in the distribution of or advising on Tokenised Securities, management of Tokenised Securities in the form of tokenised funds, management of funds investing in Tokenised Securities and secondary market trading of Tokenised Securities on virtual asset trading platforms are also governed by existing conduct requirements for securities-related activities. C. New risks arising from tokenisation 8. The overarching principle of the SFC’s regulatory approach is “same business, same risks, same rules”. In addition to complying with existing legal and regulatory requirements applicable to traditional securities, intermediaries should manage the new risks, which are not typically associated with traditional securities, especially ownership risks (eg, how ownership interest relating to the Tokenised Securities is transferred and recorded) and technology risks (eg, forking, blockchain network outages and cybersecurity risks) in activities involving tokenisation. 9. The SFC notes that there are several common archetypes of DLT networks, including: (a) private-permissioned, which is a closed-loop private network characterised by a centralised authority that controls and restricts access to predetermined users, and is typically governed by rules that apply to all users; (b) public-permissioned, which is a public network with a centralised authority that controls and restricts access through authentication, for example; and (c) public-permissionless which is an open, public network that does not restrict access for privileges and has defining characteristics such as decentralisation, pseudonymity and large-scale user base3. Risks vary depending on the type of DLT network used, and should be addressed through the implementation of adequate controls. 10. In the case of Tokenised Securities in bearer form4 issued using permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks, there may be heightened cybersecurity risks. Due to the lack of restrictions

for public access and the open nature of these networks, investors may suffer substantial losses without recourse and may also have practical difficulties recovering their assets or pursuing claims for losses in the event of theft, hacking or other cyberattacks. Further, as a result of such Tokenised Securities’ relative ease of transfer which would result in a change in ownership and their anonymity, they have potentially higher exposures to money laundering and know-your-client issues compared with Tokenised Securities in registered form. D. Considerations for engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities 11. Intermediaries engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities should have the necessary manpower and expertise to understand the nature of such businesses, especially the new risks relating to ownership and technology, and manage such risks appropriately. 12. Intermediaries should act with due skill, care and diligence, and perform due diligence on the Tokenised Securities based on all the available information to identify the key features and risks of the Tokenised Securities. This would include intermediaries’ existing obligation to conduct due diligence on the product itself (eg, on the underlying bond or fund which is being tokenised) and also on the technology aspects given the use of tokenisation technology. Issuance of Tokenised Securities 13. Where intermediaries issue (eg, fund managers of tokenised funds) or are substantially involved in the issuance of the Tokenised Securities which they intend to deal in or advise on, they remain responsible for the overall operation of the tokenisation arrangement notwithstanding any outsourcing to third-party vendors/service providers. 14. In assessing the risks related to the technical and other aspects of Tokenised Securities, an intermediary is suggested to take into account the list of non-exhaustive factors set out in Part A of the Appendix to this circular. 15. For custodial arrangements, intermediaries should take into account the features and risks of the Tokenised Securities in considering the most appropriate custodial arrangement for the Tokenised Securities to manage ownership and technology risks. Additional considerations for the custodial arrangement for bearer form Tokenised Securities which use permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks are set out in Part B of the Appendix to this circular. 16. For tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products, please also refer to the requirements under the Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products issued by the SFC. Dealing in, advising on, or managing portfolios investing in Tokenised Securities 17. Where intermediaries deal in, advise on, or manage portfolios investing in Tokenised Securities, intermediaries are reminded to conduct due diligence on the issuers and their third-party vendors/service providers involved in the tokenisation arrangement as well as the features and risks arising from the tokenisation arrangement. 18. Intermediaries should understand and be satisfied with the controls implemented by the issuers and their third-party vendors/service providers to manage ownership and technology risks of the Tokenised Securities before they engage in related activities. Please refer to Parts A and B of the Appendix to this circular for a non-exhaustive list of factors for consideration. E. Information for clients 19. Intermediaries should make adequate disclosure of relevant material information specific to Tokenised Securities (including the risks of the Tokenised Securities) and communicate such information in a clear and easily comprehensible manner. 20. Distinguish the earlier condition, interim controls and later operation. Neither absence of reported incidents nor eventual correction establishes continuous compliance; an incident does not automatically establish permanent non-compliance.

Classify the instrument, network permissions, registered or bearer form, custody chain and ownership model, including whether blockchain is only a secondary record. The Appendix is supplied and materially informs the analysis. Beyond reconciliation and custody, it addresses vendor experience, smart contracts, network robustness and attacks affecting finality, interoperability, maintained controls, legal enforceability, underlying-market effects, regulatory approval, business continuity, privacy and money-laundering risks. Its technology-audit note is delivered; it does not resolve distinct missing notes in the parent circular or target investment-product circular. Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products. A. Terminology 5. There is currently no universal definition or taxonomy for categorising tokenised securities and many different structures may exist in the market. For the purpose of this circular, tokenised securities are traditional financial instruments (eg, bonds or funds) that are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO) which utilise DLT (such as blockchain technology) or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Tokenised Securities). 6. Tokenised Securities are a subset of a broader set of digital securities, the latter of which in this circular are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the SFO that utilise DLT or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Digital Securities). Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may be structured in more bespoke, novel or complicated forms, with some existing exclusively on a DLT-based network with no links to extrinsic rights or underlying assets and having no controls to mitigate the risks that ownership rights may not be accurately recorded2. Some of them may fall under the definition of an interest in a CIS. For example, Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may include tokenisation of fractionalised interests in real world or digital assets such as artwork or land in a manner different from a traditional fund but such that the arrangement would amount to a CIS, or tokenisation of a profit sharing arrangement which is not in the form of traditional securities. B. Nature of Tokenised Securities 7. At the outset, given that the nature of Tokenised Securities are fundamentally traditional securities with a tokenisation wrapper, the existing legal and regulatory requirements governing the traditional securities markets continue to apply to Tokenised Securities. In particular, offerings of Tokenised Securities would be subject to the prospectus regime under the Companies (Winding up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32) (C(WUMP)O) and the offers of investments regime under Part IV of the SFO. Conduct of intermediaries in the distribution of or advising on Tokenised Securities, management of Tokenised Securities in the form of tokenised funds, management of funds investing in Tokenised Securities and secondary market trading of Tokenised Securities on virtual asset trading platforms are also governed by existing conduct requirements for securities-related activities. C. New risks arising from tokenisation 8. The overarching principle of the SFC’s regulatory approach is “same business, same risks, same rules”. In addition to complying with existing legal and regulatory requirements applicable to traditional securities, intermediaries should manage the new risks, which are not typically associated with traditional securities, especially ownership risks (eg, how ownership interest relating to the Tokenised Securities is transferred and recorded) and technology risks (eg, forking, blockchain network outages and cybersecurity risks) in activities involving tokenisation. 9. The SFC notes that there are several common archetypes of DLT networks, including: (a) private-permissioned, which is a closed-loop private network characterised by a centralised authority that controls and restricts access to predetermined users, and is typically governed by rules that apply to all users; (b) public-permissioned, which is a public network with a centralised authority that controls and restricts access through authentication, for example; and (c) public-permissionless which is an open, public network that does not restrict access for privileges and has defining characteristics such as decentralisation, pseudonymity and large-scale user base3. Risks vary depending on the type of DLT network used, and should be addressed through the implementation of adequate controls. 10. In the case of Tokenised Securities in bearer form4 issued using permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks, there may be heightened cybersecurity risks. Due to the lack of restrictions for public access and the open nature of these networks, investors may suffer substantial losses without recourse and may also have practical difficulties recovering their assets or pursuing claims for losses in the event of theft, hacking or other cyberattacks. Further, as a result of such Tokenised Securities’ relative ease of transfer which would result in a change in ownership and their anonymity, they have potentially higher exposures to money laundering and know-your-client issues compared with Tokenised Securities in registered form. D. Considerations for engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities 11. Intermediaries engaging in Tokenised Securities-related activities should have the necessary manpower and expertise to understand the nature of such businesses, especially the new risks relating to ownership and technology, and manage such risks appropriately. 12. Intermediaries should act with due skill, care and diligence, and perform due diligence on the Tokenised Securities based on all the available information to identify the key features and risks of the Tokenised Securities. This would include intermediaries’ existing obligation to conduct due diligence on the product itself (eg, on the underlying bond or fund which is being tokenised) and also on the technology aspects given the use of tokenisation technology. Intermediaries should act with due skill, care and diligence, and perform due diligence on the Tokenised Securities based on all the available information to identify the key features and risks of the Tokenised Securities. This would include intermediaries’ existing obligation to conduct due diligence on the product itself (eg, on the underlying bond or fund which is being tokenised) and also on the technology aspects given the use of tokenisation technology. Issuance of Tokenised Securities 13. Where intermediaries issue (eg, fund managers of tokenised funds) or are substantially involved in the issuance of the Tokenised Securities which they intend to deal in or advise on, they remain responsible for the overall operation of the tokenisation arrangement notwithstanding any outsourcing to third-party vendors/service providers. 14. In assessing the risks related to the technical and other aspects of Tokenised Securities, an intermediary is suggested to take into account the list of non-exhaustive factors set out in Part A of the Appendix to this circular. 15. For custodial arrangements, intermediaries should take into account the features and risks of the Tokenised Securities in considering the most appropriate custodial arrangement for the Tokenised Securities to manage ownership and technology risks. Additional considerations for the custodial arrangement for bearer form Tokenised Securities which use permissionless tokens on public-permissionless networks are set out in Part B of the Appendix to this circular. 16. For tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products, please also refer to the requirements under the Circular on tokenisation of SFC-authorised investment products issued by the SFC. Dealing in, advising on, or managing portfolios investing in Tokenised Securities 17. Where intermediaries deal in, advise on, or manage portfolios investing in Tokenised Securities, intermediaries are reminded to conduct due diligence on the issuers and their third-party vendors/service providers involved in the tokenisation arrangement as well as the features and risks arising from the tokenisation arrangement. 18. Intermediaries should understand and be satisfied with the controls implemented by the issuers and their third-party vendors/service providers to manage ownership and technology risks of the Tokenised Securities before they engage in related activities. Please refer to Parts A and B of the Appendix to this circular for a non-exhaustive list of factors for consideration. E. Information for clients 19. Intermediaries should make adequate disclosure of relevant material information specific to Tokenised Securities (including the risks of the Tokenised Securities) and communicate such information in a clear and easily comprehensible manner. 20. Intermediaries are expected to provide clients with material information on the tokenisation arrangement, for example: (a) whether off-chain or on-chain settlement is final; (b) the limitations imposed on transfers of the Tokenised Securities (if any); (c) whether a smart contract audit has been conducted before deployment of the smart contract (if any); (d) key administrative controls and business continuity planning for DLT-related events5; and (e) the custodial arrangement (if applicable). 6.11    Offer and redemption prices should be calculated on the basis of the scheme's net asset
        value divided by the number of units/shares outstanding. Such prices should fairly reflect
        the value of a scheme’s assets and may be adjusted by fees and charges, provided the
        amount or method of calculating such fees and charges is clearly disclosed in the
        offering document.

6.11A The management company should establish appropriate policies and procedures for
      independent valuation of each type of assets held by a scheme in consultation with the
      trustee/custodian. Such policies and procedures should seek to detect, prevent and
      correct pricing errors and be consistently applied. The management company should
      review the valuation policies and procedures on a periodic basis to ensure their
      continued appropriateness and effective implementation. The valuation policies,
      procedures and process should be reviewed (at least annually) by a competent and
      functionally-independent party such as a qualified independent third party or a person
      performing an independent audit function.

        Notes: (1)     Where fair value adjustments are necessary in view that market value of
                       a scheme’s assets is unavailable, or reasonably considered to be not
                       reliable or reflective of an exit price upon current sale, the management
                       company shall conduct such adjustments with due skill, care and
                       diligence, and in good faith. The process and conduct of fair value
                       adjustments should be done by the management company in consultation
                       with the trustee/custodian.

               (2)     The management company must comply with all applicable legal and
                       regulatory requirements in respect of the valuation of a scheme’s assets.

               (3)     For the purpose of satisfying the requirement on independent review of
                       valuation policies, procedures and process, the review should include
                       testing the valuation procedures by which scheme assets are valued. The
                       management company shall exercise due skill, care and diligence in the

6.11B Assets of a scheme should be valued on a regular basis and in any event, on the days
      that the scheme’s units/shares are offered or redeemed in accordance with the
      constitutive documents. Valuation frequency and the basis of valuation of a scheme’s
      assets should be clearly disclosed in the offering document.

6.11C Where a third party is engaged in the valuation of a scheme, the management company
      shall exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence in the selection, appointment and
      ongoing monitoring of such third party in ensuring such entity possesses the appropriate
      level of knowledge, experience and resources that commensurate with the appropriate
      valuation policies and procedures for each scheme. The valuation activities of such third
      party should be subject to ongoing supervision and periodic review by the management
      company.

There is currently no universal definition or taxonomy for categorising tokenised securities and many different structures may exist in the market. For the purpose of this circular, tokenised securities are traditional financial instruments (eg, bonds or funds) that are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the Securities and Futures Ordinance (Cap. 571) (SFO) which utilise DLT (such as blockchain technology) or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Tokenised Securities). 6. Tokenised Securities are a subset of a broader set of digital securities, the latter of which in this circular are “securities” as defined in section 1 of Part 1 of Schedule 1 to the SFO that utilise DLT or similar technology in their security lifecycle (Digital Securities). Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may be structured in more bespoke, novel or complicated forms, with some existing exclusively on a DLT-based network with no links to extrinsic rights or underlying assets and having no controls to mitigate the risks that ownership rights may not be accurately recorded2. Some of them may fall under the definition of an interest in a CIS. For example, Digital Securities which are not Tokenised Securities may include tokenisation of fractionalised interests in real world or digital assets such as artwork or land in a manner different from a traditional fund but such that the arrangement would amount to a CIS, or tokenisation of a profit sharing arrangement which is not in the form of traditional securities. B. Nature of Tokenised Securities 7. At the outset, given that the nature of Tokenised Securities are fundamentally traditional securities with a tokenisation wrapper, the existing legal and regulatory requirements governing the traditional securities markets continue to apply to Tokenised Securities. In particular, offerings of Tokenised Securities would be subject to the prospectus regime under the Companies (Winding up and Miscellaneous Provisions) Ordinance (Cap. 32) (C(WUMP)O) and the offers of investments regime under Part IV of the SFO. Conduct of intermediaries in the distribution of or advising on Tokenised Securities, management of Tokenised Securities in the form of tokenised funds, management of funds investing in Tokenised Securities and secondary market trading of Tokenised Securities on virtual asset trading platforms are also governed by existing conduct requirements for securities-related activities. C. New risks arising from tokenisation 8. The overarching principle of the SFC’s regulatory approach is “same business, same risks, same rules”. In addition to complying with existing legal and regulatory requirements applicable to traditional securities, intermediaries should manage the new risks, which are not typically associated with traditional securities, especially ownership risks (eg, how ownership interest relating to the Tokenised Securities is transferred and recorded) and technology risks (eg, forking, blockchain network outages and cybersecurity risks) in activities involving tokenisation. 9.       review the valuation policies and procedures on a periodic basis to ensure their
      continued appropriateness and effective implementation. The valuation policies,
      procedures and process should be reviewed (at least annually) by a competent and
      functionally-independent party such as a qualified independent third party or a person
      performing an independent audit function.

alternatives.consequence: The contract supports an allocation of responsibility on paper. It does not establish effective retained authority, actual supervision or fulfillment. Neither compliance nor breach is established on these facts.

alternatives.condition: Executed agreements and governance arrangements show that the Provider retains effective decision-making, information-access and intervention powers appropriate to the applicable requirement.
alternatives.consequence: Those materials could support retained authority in substance, rather than merely contractual acceptance. Review delegated functions, reserved decisions, reporting rights and practical ability to intervene. These are proposed evidentiary inquiries, not a verified universal legal test.

alternatives.condition: Contemporaneous evidence shows that the Provider actually exercised the supervision required by the applicable standard.
alternatives.consequence: Due-diligence files, reporting and review records, decisions, escalations and remediation evidence could support fulfillment of the relevant conduct obligations. The existence of a reporting process or a single recorded action does not itself establish adequate supervision; its scope, timing and response must be assessed against the governing standard.

alternatives.condition: Operational and record-keeping evidence demonstrates the outcomes required by an applicable rule.
alternatives.consequence: Control tests, incident records, reconciliations and evidence of corrective action could support fulfillment of those outcome or record-keeping requirements. Successful operations alone do not prove proper allocation or supervision; an adverse incident alone does not establish breach of a care-and-diligence obligation. The governing standard determines the significance of each.

alternatives.condition: The supplied Handbook requirements govern this Provider, product and engagement at the relevant time.
alternatives.consequence: Selection of counterparties and service providers must be assessed for reasonable care and diligence. For key counterparties and service providers, the Provider must also satisfy itself through due enquiries concerning competence and resources to discharge their engagement obligations and comply with relevant applicable product-code requirements. Contractual acceptance of responsibility does not demonstrate those enquiries or their adequacy.

Chapter 5: General requirements
      Name of product

5.1   A products name shall not be undesirable or misleading.

      Notes:        Issuers should consider the following factors before selecting the name for a
                    product:

                    (i)     whether it is inconsistent with the nature of the product or the
                            investment objectives or policy of the product;

                    (ii)    whether the name of the product would give investors a sense of
                            assurance or security not justified by the underlying features of the
                            product;

                    (iii)   whether it might lead investors into thinking or create the impression
                            that persons other than the Product Provider are responsible for the
                            product; and

                    (iv)    whether it might lead investors into thinking or create the impression
                            that the Product Provider is not responsible for the product.

5.2   Where the name of a product includes the word guaranteed, principal protected,
      capital protected or words with similar meanings, it shall accurately reflect the nature
      and extent of the guarantee or the capital/principal protection taking into account the
      impression that such description might give to the investing public.

      Selection of distributors

5.3   The Product Provider shall exercise reasonable care and diligence in the selection and
      appointment of distributors for a product, in particular, having regard to whether such
      distributor is suitably qualified and competent to discharge its obligations properly.

      Engagement of counterparties and appointment of service providers

5.4   The Product Provider shall exercise reasonable care and diligence in the selection of
      counterparties and service providers.

5.5   The Product Provider shall satisfy itself, having made due enquiries, that each of the key
      counterparties and service providers engaged or appointed in respect of the product is
      competent and has resources to:

      (a)      duly discharge its obligations under its terms of engagement or appointment; and

      (b)      comply with all relevant requirements set out in applicable product code
               specifically applicable to such counterparties/service providers.

      Language

5.6   Without prejudice to any requirement under applicable laws, all offering documents shall
      be written in both the Chinese and English languages, unless this requirement is
      otherwise waived by the Commission.
